notes.meaning: Good king Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem. His son Jehoram took the throne after having already served for a time alongside his father as co-king. Even though Jehoram had a godly father, he chose a completely different path once he had full power.

Jehoshaphat had six other sons whom he loved and provided for during his lifetime. The text calls Jehoshaphat the king of Israel because all the people of Judah belonged to the family of Israel, and many faithful Israelites from the northern tribes had moved to Judah. Two brothers shared the name Azariah, but their names were spelled slightly differently to tell them apart.

Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons generous gifts of gold and silver, and put them in charge of fortified towns. This was a wise plan meant to give them meaningful work and keep them away from the capital so they would not fight over the throne. Because Jehoram was the eldest son, he inherited the crown.

As soon as Jehoram felt secure as the sole ruler, he murdered all six of his brothers along with several royal leaders. He did this out of jealousy and fear, hardening his heart to remove any possible challenge to his power. His cruelty showed how completely evil and insecure his rule would be.

Jehoram began his sole reign when he was thirty-two years old and ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. His short time on the throne was marked by disaster and rebellion from start to finish. Power gained through bloodshed brought him no lasting peace.

Jehoram rejected the good examples of his father and grandfather and copied the wicked kings of the northern kingdom of Israel instead. He had married Athaliah, the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, and her pagan ways heavily influenced him. Bad companions and an ungodly marriage led him directly into open rebellion against God.

Jehoram deserved to have his royal house wiped out, but the Lord spared it for the sake of His covenant with David. A covenant is a sacred, unbreakable promise sealed by God. The Lord had promised David that a lamp, meaning an unbroken line of royal descendants leading to the future Messiah, would never be completely put out.

The nation of Edom had paid tribute to Judah since the days of King David. Seeing Judah's spiritual and moral decay under Jehoram, the Edomites revolted and set up their own king. When God's blessing left the king, his foreign territories began to break away.

Jehoram led his military commanders and chariots to crush the Edomite rebellion. The Edomite forces managed to surround his troops, forcing Jehoram to launch a desperate night counterattack just to cut his way out. Although he escaped with his life, he failed to regain control of Edom.

Edom won its permanent freedom from Judah, and the border city of Libnah broke away at the same time. The text explains that these losses happened because Jehoram had abandoned the Lord, the God of his ancestors. When the king stopped honoring God, his own subjects stopped honoring his authority.

Jehoram built pagan shrines on the hills of Judah and pushed his subjects into idolatry. The Bible calls this spiritual prostitution because worshiping false gods breaks faith with the Lord, just as adultery breaks the marriage promise. Jehoram even used royal force and penalties to compel his people to turn from God.

Jehoram received a written letter of warning from the prophet Elijah. Elijah had likely written this message by the Holy Spirit before being taken to heaven, leaving it to be delivered when Jehoram fell into wicked ways. The letter confronted the king directly with the fact that he had refused to follow the godly examples of Asa and Jehoshaphat.

The letter listed Jehoram's two greatest sins: promoting Baal worship like the house of Ahab, and murdering his own brothers. God declared that those murdered brothers were better men than Jehoram, being far more righteous and faithful. His crime was not just murder, but an attack against those who loved the Lord.

God warned that a terrible blow was about to fall upon Jehoram's kingdom, his family, and his wealth. Because the people followed along with his pagan practices, they too would face hardship. The king would watch his entire household and kingdom suffer ruin under God's judgment.

Elijah's letter announced that Jehoram would suffer a terrible, lingering sickness of his bowels. This was a fitting penalty for a man who showed no compassion or pity toward his own brothers. The disease would cause intense daily suffering until it brought about his death.

The Lord stirred up foreign enemies, including the Philistines and neighboring Arab tribes, to attack Judah. These nations had previously lived in peace under Jehoshaphat, but God now used them as instruments of judgment. National defense crumbled because the nation had turned away from the Lord.

The invaders broke into Judah, ransacked the royal palace, and captured Jehoram's wives and older sons. The raiders murdered his older sons, leaving only his youngest son, Jehoahaz, alive. Jehoram had killed all his brothers to secure his throne, and now all his own sons except one were stripped away from him.

After the foreign invasion, God struck Jehoram's body with the incurable intestinal sickness that Elijah had prophesied. No physician or medicine could heal what God had sent as a direct judgment. His outer physical ruin mirrored the deep corruption of his soul.

Jehoram suffered in severe agony for two years until his intestines ruptured and he died. Because he was an oppressive and ungodly ruler, his subjects made no ceremonial bonfire of spices in his honor, a tribute normally given to good kings. His painful end proved that God's warnings through Elijah were completely true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the Hebrew phrasing might describe a sudden collapse over two days rather than two continuous years of illness.

notes.meaning: Jehoram died at forty years old, and absolutely no one mourned his passing. He was buried in Jerusalem, but the people refused him a place in the royal tombs reserved for honored kings of David's line. A selfish life spent fighting against God left behind only shame and disgrace.
